extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in psychology and related fields studying humor and emotion; social/experimental psychologists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts/principles from an academic theory explaining when events are perceived as humorous (the 'benign violations' account) and the social/communicative functions of humor. Targets empirical and theoretical work on what makes things funny and how laughter functions socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a response to benign violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor provides a healthy and socially beneficial way to react to hypothetical threats, remote concerns, minor setbacks, social faux pas, cultural misunderstandings, and other benign violations people encounter on a regular basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat events that are violations of expectation/norms as potential humor stimuli only when they are perceived as 'benign' (non-threatening or acceptable in context). This principle frames which kinds of events are likely to elicit amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate functional targets of humor (coping/mitigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor provides a healthy and socially beneficial way to react to hypothetical threats, remote concerns, minor setbacks, social faux pas, cultural misunderstandings, and other benign violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating humorous content, consider whether it helps individuals cope with or reframe threats/concerns and whether it targets relatively low-cost, non-immediate harms (e.g., minor setbacks, faux pas). Humor that serves these coping/mitigation functions is more socially beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative signaling function of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and amusement signal to the world that a violation is indeed okay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or interpret laughter not only as private affect but as a social signal indicating acceptability of a previously problematic or norm-violating event; evaluate whether laughter is being used to reassure observers that a violation is benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about gender effects in amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Across the five studies, there was no consistent evidence for gender effects. When they were present, women tended to be less amused than men; this could have been due to stimulus selection or socially desirable responding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume robust gender differences in amusement without checking for confounds (stimulus selection, demand characteristics, social desirability). Treat observed gender differences as tentative and investigate alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus selection and unintended benign violations
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed amusement in a control condition may be due to unintended semantic or cultural associations (example: the brand name 'Hummer' can be used as a euphemism for a sexual act, creating an unintended benign violation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or selecting stimuli for humor research or producing humorous content, screen for unintended meanings, euphemisms, or cultural associations that could create unplanned benign violations and confound results or audience reactions.
